query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a controlled phase-selective recrystallization annealing treatment on an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) will fully recrystallize the soft FCC lamellae while retaining the hard B2 (or ordered BCC) phase network, thereby significantly reducing dislocation pile-ups at internal FCC/B2 interfaces and mitigating local stress concentrations.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure composed of soft FCC and hard B2 phases that exhibits pronounced dislocation pile-ups at internal phase boundaries, leading to limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness.
generation.intervention: A single thermal annealing treatment designed for phase-selective recrystallization. The alloy will be heated to an optimized temperature (approximately 700°C) for a controlled duration (for example, 10–20 minutes) and then cooled at a controlled rate to ensure full recrystallization of the FCC phase without compromising the hard-phase framework.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing under quasi-static loading (e.g., strain-rate ~10^(-3) s^(−1)) and in situ microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM or EBSD) to assess dislocation distributions.
generation.structural_mediator: A fully recrystallized FCC lamellar structure with minimized dislocation storage sites and coherent/semi-coherent interfaces to the retained B2 phase, leading to a more uniform distribution of plastic deformation.
generation.mechanism: By eliminating the unrecrystallized soft FCC regions that are prone to accumulating dislocations, the thermal treatment redistributes and homogenizes the dislocation density. This minimizes local stress concentrations at the phase boundaries, delays the initiation of microcracks, and promotes both effective work hardening and improved ductility. Meanwhile, the hard B2 phase continues to provide high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy (which might exhibit a yield strength around 500 MPa and uniform elongation below 10%), the treated alloy is expected to show an increase in yield strength by approximately 25–50% (e.g., reaching between 625 and 750 MPa) and an improvement in uniform tensile ductility by potentially more than 300% (for instance, achieving >30% elongation), thereby overcoming brittleness without sacrificing strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy with its original hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure shows limited room-temperature tensile ductility (<10% uniform elongation) and brittleness due to dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the phase-selective recrystallization is contingent upon achieving selective recrystallization of the FCC phase without inducing excessive grain growth or degradation of the hard B2 framework; deviations in the temperature-time profile may lead either to incomplete recrystallization (leaving dislocation pile-ups intact) or to coarsening that adversely affects strength.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing temperature and duration for selective recrystallization may be narrow and alloy-specific. There is also uncertainty regarding the potential for over-recrystallization or phase coarsening, which could offset the benefits. Finally, minor variations in alloy composition may impact the reproducibility of the targeted microstructural changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of as-cast eutectic HEA specimens and another set subjected to the phase-selective recrystallization treatment as described. Perform in situ tensile tests (with concurrent TEM or high-resolution EBSD mapping) to directly observe dislocation distributions, interface behavior, and microcrack initiation under identical room-temperature quasi-static loading conditions.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength via standard mechanical testing
Dislocation density and distribution at FCC/B2 interfaces (using TEM/EBSD)
Onset and propagation of microcracks (monitored in situ)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries and do not show improved tensile ductility and/or strength (i.e., if mechanical properties are similar to or worse than the untreated specimens), or if microcrack initiation is not delayed relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:The role of phase boundary in second phase strengthening
cited_evidence.text: It is a traditional method to strengthen alloys by introducing internal boundaries in order to impede the motion of dislocations. Unlike coherent twin boundaries with low excess energies, grain boundaries and phase boundaries are regarded as major strengthening agents for metallic materials because they are more effective in resisting dislocation penetration. In this study, the phase boundaries were produced through the eutectic reaction during the preparation of dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA. Thereby plenty of phase boundaries contained in this HEA were semi-coherent due to the low energy features. Given that interfacial strength increases with the decrease of coherency, phase boundaries of semi-coherence prepared in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were observed to be strong enough to accommodate high stress due to their chemically disordered features, as proved by the HAADF-STEM observation (Fig. 3b) and in-situ straining experiments. Such strong phase boundaries were essential to achieving compatibility of interphase deformations through enhancing the strength of FCC phases by work hardening effects so as to commence dislocation glide in BCC phases.

In the hierarchical structure, there are coarse non-lamellar regions featuring a mixture of soft FCC and hard B2 phases. Although these regions allow significant strain partitioning to induce back-stress strengthening, the soft FCC phase also allows the material to yield at low stress, owning to the absence of the lamellar constraint effect. That is why a previous hierarchical structure shows a limited improvement in the yield strength compared to the corresponding ultrafine-grained EHEA. Recently, Yang et al. reported work in a single-phase medium-entropy alloy, where they purposely architectured a three-level heterogeneous grain structure with grain sizes spanning the nanometer-to-micrometer range via partial recrystallization annealing following conventional cold-rolling, achieving large uniform tensile strain (~22%) after yielding even at the gigapascal stress. They attributed these improved properties to high back-stress strengthening caused by structurally inhomogeneous deformation characteristics. Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. papers.title: The Exceptional Strong Face-centered Cubic Phase and Semi-coherent Phase Boundary in a Eutectic Dual-phase High Entropy Alloy AlCoCrFeNi.
papers.system: Eutectic dual‐phase HEA (AlCoCrFeNi) with FCC and BCC lamellae produced by casting.
papers.approach: In situ deformation experiments to observe dislocation substructures and phase boundary effects.
papers.findings: Observed that despite the intrinsically hard BCC phase, the pre‐strained FCC phase developed dense dislocation networks near semi‐coherent phase boundaries. The strong, chemically disordered interfaces reduced dislocation penetration and pile‐ups, thereby mitigating stress concentration and delaying crack propagation.
papers.mechanism: Semi-coherent phase boundaries serve as barriers that not only block dislocations but also enhance dislocation accumulation in the FCC phase, promoting work hardening while limiting the tendency for catastrophic microcracking.

papers.title: Enhanced strength-ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae.
papers.system: Eutectic HEA (AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with inherited dual-phase lamellar composite microstructure processed via thermo-mechanical treatments.
papers.approach: Tailored thermomechanical processing to create an ultrafine heterogeneous microstructure with lamellar and non-lamellar domains, then in situ observations and tensile testing.
papers.findings: The engineered heterogeneous structure promoted strain partitioning and strong back-stress hardening. However, dislocation pile-ups near lamellar interfaces were also noted as potential sites for microcrack initiation if the interface integrity declined.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between soft FCC and hard B2 (or BCC) phases builds up local strain gradients leading to geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) that enhance work hardening, but may also concentrate stresses at internal boundaries.

papers.title: Phase-selective recrystallization makes eutectic high-entropy alloys ultra-ductile.
papers.system: Eutectic HEA with duplex phases (soft FCC and hard phase skeleton) designed for improved ductility.
papers.approach: A distinctive phase-selective recrystallization treatment to fully recrystallize the soft phase while retaining a hard phase framework.
papers.findings: The resulting microstructure exhibited a high ductility (~35% uniform elongation) and a high true stress (~2 GPa). By selectively recrystallizing the ductile phase, the treatment mitigated the adverse effects of weak boundaries and reduced stress concentration associated with dislocation pile-ups.
papers.mechanism: Elimination of weak boundaries in the soft phase reduces sites for dislocation pile-ups and microcrack initiation, while maintaining the high strength provided by the retained hard-phase skeleton.

papers.title: Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing.
papers.system: Nano-lamellar eutectic HEA (AlCoCrFeNi2.1) processed starting from cast state followed by cryo-rolling and subsequent annealing.
papers.approach: A combination of cryo-rolling (to store dislocations) followed by annealing to produce a hierarchical microstructure with refined soft and hard regions.
papers.findings: The processed alloy achieved significantly improved yield strength (~1437 MPa) and ductility (~14% elongation) relative to untreated cast material, attributed to a dual-phase microstructure that better accommodated strain and limited catastrophic microcracking.
papers.mechanism: Tailored deformation and annealing treatment generates nano-lamellae that promote distributed dislocation storage and back-stress hardening, reducing dislocation pile‐up localization at phase boundaries.

papers.title: Nanodomained Nickel Unite Nanocrystal Strength with Coarse-Grain Ductility.
papers.system: Nanostructured pure Ni via defect engineering introducing nanoscale domains in a coarse-grained matrix.
papers.approach: Introduction of nanodomains to act as dislocation obstacles; post-mortem TEM analysis to capture dislocation bowing and pile-ups at domain boundaries.
papers.findings: Nanodomains provided dual functionality by impeding dislocation motion (raising strength) and serving as sources for dislocation emission. However, notable dislocation pile-ups at the nanodomain boundaries were observed, which, if uncontrolled, could lead to local stress concentrations.
papers.mechanism: Dislocation bowing around nanoscale domains increases internal dislocation density and work hardening, offering insights for similar interventions in multiphase alloys.

established: Eutectic HEAs can be engineered to exhibit a composite dual-phase lamellar microstructure combining soft (FCC) and hard (BCC/B2) phases.
Semi-coherent and chemically disordered phase boundaries can enhance work hardening by limiting dislocation penetration and storage.
Interface characteristics and domain boundaries play a critical role in controlling dislocation pile-ups that lead to local stresses and microcracking.
Heterogeneous microstructures can enable back-stress strengthening, delaying necking and enhancing ductility.

approaches_tried.approach: Tailored thermomechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling and annealing) to modify microstructure.
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved enhanced strength (higher YS and UTS) and moderate ductility by producing a hierarchical, nano-lamellar structure that distributes strains and back stresses.

approaches_tried.approach: Phase-selective recrystallization to convert soft phase into a fully recrystallized state embedded in a strong hard phase network.
approaches_tried.outcome: Resulted in ultra-ductile behavior with improved work hardening capacity and high strength (~2 GPa true stress), overcoming limitations in the as-cast microstructure.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ defect engineering by introducing nanodomains to block dislocations.
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced strength via dislocation bowing and increased storage; however, excessive dislocation pile-ups can also trigger local stress concentrations.

mechanisms: Semi-coherent phase boundaries blocking dislocation motion and enhancing dislocation storage in compliant phases.
Back-stress hardening arising from strain gradients at interfaces between soft and hard domains.
Dislocation bowing around nanoscale obstacles and redistribution of dislocation density to delay crack nucleation.
Phase-selective recrystallization reducing weak interfacial regions where dislocation pile-ups concentrate.
disagreements: Traditional approaches emphasizing increased hard phase volume (e.g., BCC) versus findings that reducing hard-phase proportion can enhance overall strength by promoting beneficial dislocation interactions in the FCC phase.
The balance between beneficial work hardening (via GNDs and back stresses) and the detrimental effect of localized dislocation pile-ups causing microcracking remains debated.
open_questions: What single intervention can effectively mitigate local stress concentrations from dislocation pile-ups along internal phase boundaries in eutectic HEAs?
How can processing be optimized to rearrange or modify the internal boundaries so that they promote uniform strain distribution without initiating microcracks?
What are the quantitative effects of such interventions on strength and ductility relative to the untreated dual-phase eutectic structure under room-temperature conditions?
opportunities: Investigate a targeted thermal-mechanical treatment (e.g., an optimized phase-selective recrystallization procedure) designed to relieve or redistribute dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries without compromising the high-strength hard phase framework.

Explore interface engineering strategies such as minor alloying or heat treatment to modify the chemical disorder at phase boundaries, thereby enhancing their capacity to continuously store dislocations while minimizing local stress concentrations.

Develop in situ testing protocols at room temperature to assess the evolution of dislocation densities at internal boundaries and correlate microstructural modifications with improvements in tensile ductility and strength.

Combine interventions (e.g., cryo-rolling followed by controlled annealing with phase-selective recrystallization) to fine-tune the hierarchical lamellar microstructure and establish a clear structure-property relationship that can be falsified by deliberately degrading phase boundary coherence.

directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the weak, unrecrystallized soft FCC lamellae that accumulate excessive dislocations at the boundaries. By fully recrystallizing the soft phase while maintaining the integrity of the hard phase (B2), dislocation pile‐ups and local stress concentrations can be alleviated. It is supported by prior evidence (e.g., PMC9365806, PMC6175879) and is feasible with controlled annealing parameters.

Cryo-rolling, followed by a subsequent annealing treatment, can produce a refined, hierarchically structured nano-lamellar morphology, which has been shown to enhance strength and ductility (see PMC5818523). However, this method may still leave some internal boundaries that serve as stress concentrators, making it a less direct solution to the dislocation pile-up issue.

Adding trace amounts of elements (such as Ti or Nb) that segregate to phase boundaries could tailor the interface chemistry and reduce the barrier for dislocation transfer. Although promising, the effect on the overall phase stability and the narrow processing window make this intervention less straightforward and more uncertain compared to a targeted thermal treatment.

directions.direction: Controlled partial recrystallization to create gradient microstructures
directions.assessment: A strategy that involves partial recrystallization could induce a gradient of grain sizes and phases to promote back-stress hardening and distributed deformation. While it can moderate dislocation pile-ups, it may not completely remove the weak internal boundaries, and its effects on uniform tensile ductility are less directly predictable.

directions.direction: Surface modification via laser shock peening
directions.assessment: Laser shock peening can induce compressive residual stresses that help delay crack initiation by reducing local tensile stresses at the boundaries. However, as a surface treatment, it may not sufficiently address the bulk microstructural dislocation pile-ups responsible for brittle failure.

choice.why: This intervention directly remediates the problematic internal boundaries by fully recrystallizing the soft FCC phase while preserving the reinforcing hard phase. The approach is supported by existing studies (e.g., PMC9365806 and PMC6175879) showing dramatic improvements in ductility and strength. Its singular step nature also meets the requirement of a 'single intervention' and is achievable with precise thermal control.
